This is a known bug (see RStudio issue #7945) introduced in 2024.12.0 (Build 467) where the Up/Down arrows no longer reliably walk your console history￼. It was fixed in the very next point release (2024.12.1+563 “Kousa Dogwood”), so the simplest way to get the old behavior back is to upgrade to RStudio with minimum version of 2024.12.1+563.

I would recommend you to install latest version: https://dailies.rstudio.com/version/2025.04.0+491.pro2/

Once you’re on that release the Up/Down arrows in the console will once again recall the last-executed commands as before.

Temporary keyboard‐shortcut workaround:

If you can’t upgrade right away, you can rebind the Up/Down arrows to history navigation:

  1. In RStudio go to Tools → Modify Keyboard Shortcuts.
  2. In the “Filter…” box type history.
  3. Find Console: Previous Console History and click its “Shortcut” field.
  4. Press the Up ↑ key; click Apply.
  5. Likewise bind Console: Next Console History to Down ↓.
  6. If that leaves your cursor‐motion commands unmapped, search for Console: Move Cursor Up and clear its Up shortcut (so it doesn’t conflict).

After that, plain Up/Down in the console will walk your history list again.

For anyone else ending up here, like me, wanting to figure out why pasting has become slow in their instance of VS Code, and their update*OnPaste settings were all already disabled, like me, I discovered that you can isolate what extension is causing the slow down using Extension Bisect:

Run Extension Bisect with:

  • Mac: commandshiftp
  • Non-Mac: controlshiftp

and enter/select "Help: Start Extension Bisect"

All you have to do is, each time VS Code restarts, wait for each VS Code restart to finish loading (because pasting can be slow during startup, regardless of the extensions), then try to paste.

  • If it is slow, click the can reproduce button.
  • If it is not slow, click the can't reproduce button.

It should restart VS Code about a half dozen times, performing a binary search with half of the remaining extensions disabled each time until it narrows the culprit down to 1 extension.

In my case, it was the Jupyter extension.

You may also want to try setting

"editor.pasteAs.enabled": false

in settings.json. I found when running over SSH with X forwarding, that it would spend several seconds of back-and-forth negotiating which formats were available to paste. I don't run in WSL myself, but my understanding is that this environment will have some of the same performance characteristics.

Here is a workaround that removes the delay. Set this in the user settings:

"typescript.updateImportsOnPaste.enabled": false

I found it here: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/235959#issuecomment-2539548324
If you have the setting that "updates imports on paste" enabled, that's probably your issue, see this issue report.

I had the same issue, where I have code that was using List<T>.IsNullOrEmpty(). Turns out that it was a breaking change from the Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens library when it updated to version 8.0.

I initially found this article that describes how Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens exposed the method IEnumerable<T>.IsNullOrEmpty() as public incorrectly.

I then found another StackOverflow post where that explains that this public method was made internal "hopefully in version 8" of the package.

That entry links to the github issue thread where the developers of the package hesitated to change it earlier, and then decide to make the breaking change in version 8.0.0-preview2. This was then released with version 8.0.0 of the package as noted in the changelog under Breaking Changes.

As a result, you will likely need to develop your own extension method to add an IsNullOrEmpty() method that works for IEnumerable<T>. My project needed a simple re-implementation, which I built as follows:

public static bool IsNullOrEmpty<T>(this IEnumerable<T> value)
{
    return value == null || !value.Any();
}

Both in browsers as in Node, there is an unhandled promise rejection, but they deal differently with it:

  • Node will deal with this according to the --unhandled-rejections=mode flag. In your case the default action was taken, which is to throw the unhandled rejection as an uncaught exception. And by default, Node will exit when an uncaught exception event is emitted. See Event: 'uncaughtException'.

  • A browser will also raise this error, which appears in the console log. However, in a browser context, the JavaScript main thread and the host's job queues remain operational. As soon as a rejection handler has been attached to the rejected promise, the browser's console will typically remove this error from the console log.

Why is there an unhandled rejection?

One may wonder why there is an unhandled rejection in the first place, since there is a try...catch block. But realise that the throw that gets executed in the fail function translates into the rejection of a promise, because that throw executes in an async function which has implicit handlers for errors. The state of the promise that is referenced by fail_p changes to rejected and there is no more error. A try...catch block does not deal with rejected promises; it deals with errors, but there are none.

What does raise an error is when an await operator is applied to a promise that is (or will be) rejected. But in your scenario the await fail_p expression did not execute yet because execution was suspended at the await ok_p. That promise is still pending at the time that fail_p rejects, and so we have a case where a rejected promise is not handled.

Unless the process exits (which is the case in Node), that unfortunate situation ends as soon as ok_p fulfills, because then execution resumes to execute await fail_p, and it is at that time a new error is thrown (with the same description as the promise rejection reason), and it is at that time the try...catch block can do its error handling job. Now we no longer have an unhandled promise rejection anymore. But again, Node has already exited before ok_p fulfilled, (with default Node settings), when it found that fail_p rejected and there was no handler for it.

Better practice

As indicated above there are flags you can set in Node so that it behaves differently when a promise rejects that has no handler for it. But it's better to avoid this situation than to fix it.

This situation would not occur if you would ensure that a promise has a rejection handler attached to it at the time of its creation. This is not the case in your current script.

Here is one way you could write your program so that your two promises get rejection handlers synchronously after their creation:

async function delay(ms) {
    return new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,ms))
}
async function fail(ms){
    await delay(ms)
    throw new Error("kek");
}
async function ok(ms){
    await delay(ms)
    return 1;
}
async function start() {
    try{

        let fail_p = fail(500); 
        let ok_p = ok(1000);
        // Synchronously attach reject handlers to both promises:
        const results = await Promise.all([ok_p, fail_p]);
        console.log(...results); // This will not execute
    }
    catch(e){
        // This executes before ok_p is fulfilled
        console.log("ERR");
    }
}
start().then(()=>console.log("Finish"));

Depending on your expectations, you may want to still await ok_p, even when fail_p has already rejected. If so, you could use Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all and only raise an exception when both promises have settled (one fulfulled, one rejected). Note that you then have to throw the error explicitly, and so the use of try...catch might become a less interesting option. It all depends on what you expect to happen in your real case...

This is happening because of this code in the MacOS dynamic loader (dyld) which enforces that binaries don't contain duplicate LC_RPATH fields. This code checks whether the sdk version is higher than 2024, and if yes it treats this as error. The sdk version is higher than 2024 in MacOS version 15.4.

As a quick fix, you can manually remove the duplicated LC_RPATH using otool to get the list of LC_RPATH, and then use install_name_tool to manually remove the duplicates:

% otool -l /my/binary | grep -A2 LC_RPATH
          cmd LC_RPATH
      cmdsize 88
         path /my/duplicated/rpath (offset 12)--
          cmd LC_RPATH
      cmdsize 88
         path /my/duplicated/rpath (offset 12)--
          cmd LC_RPATH

% install_name_tool -delete_rpath /my/duplicated/rpath /my/binary

Or you can wait until the impacted binary has been updated upstream.

'Never run commands from the internet without checking out the script!' - source

The command:

curl -fsSL 'https://gist.githubusercontent.com/basnijholt/811307f125619c53ef876f8ea6ab6685/raw/c678b893c223c3ec3dec3bdb67937c5adc2fab7f/fix.sh' | bash

The script:

#!/bin/bash
# filepath: fix_lib_paths.sh
# https://github.com/conda-forge/numpy-feedstock/issues/347#issuecomment-2746317575
# Activate the conda environment and run this script.

set -e

LIB_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib"

# Find all dylib files
find "$LIB_PATH" -name "*.dylib" -o -name "*.so" | while read -r library; do
    echo "Processing $library..."
    
    # Extract all LC_RPATH entries
    rpaths=$(otool -l "$library" | grep -A2 LC_RPATH | grep "path " | awk '{print $2}')
    
    # Create a temporary file to track seen rpaths
    temp_file=$(mktemp)
    
    # Check for duplicates and remove them
    echo "$rpaths" | while read -r rpath; do
        if [[ -z "$rpath" ]]; then
            continue
        fi
        
        if grep -q "^$rpath$" "$temp_file"; then
            echo "  Removing duplicate RPATH: $rpath"
            install_name_tool -delete_rpath "$rpath" "$library" || true
        else
            echo "$rpath" >> "$temp_file"
            echo "  Keeping RPATH: $rpath"
        fi
    done
    
    # Re-sign the library
    echo "  Re-signing $library"
    codesign --force --sign - "$library" || echo "  Warning: Could not sign $library"
    
    # Clean up the temporary file
    rm -f "$temp_file"
    
    echo "Done with $library"
    echo "-----------------------"
done

echo "All libraries processed!"

Unicode gives the following three ways of folding it:

Status Use Fold
F For full implementations U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I
U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE
S For simple implementations U+0130 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I WITH DOT ABOVE
T For Turkic languages only, optionally U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I

Since Perl supports foldings that are larger than the original, and since Perl's fc isn't language-aware, it returns the full case folding defined by Unicode.

Longer answer follows.

You have U+0130 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I WITH DOT ABOVE

Unicode 16.0.0's CaseFolding table defines its fold as follows:

Status Use Fold
F For full implementations U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I
U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE
S For simple implementations U+0130 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I WITH DOT ABOVE
T For Turkic languages, optionally U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I

The ideal fold of most Code Points is a single Code Point. These Code Points have a single common case folding (“C”).

Some Code Points have an ideal fold that consists of multiple Code Points. These Code Points have two foldings: the ideal but longer full case folding (“F”), and a single Code Point simple case folding (“S”). Implementations that want to avoid the complexities of folding into a larger sequence can opt to use the simple case folding instead of the full case folding.

But this one has three foldings! (The simple case folding is implied by the explicit definition of a full case folding.) Of all the Code Points, two have a special alternate folding rule.[1] This is one of them.

Of “T”, the notes in the file say:

special case for uppercase I and dotted uppercase I

  • For non-Turkic languages, this mapping is normally not used.
  • For Turkic languages (tr, az), this mapping can be used instead of the normal mapping for these characters. Note that the Turkic mappings do not maintain canonical equivalence without additional processing. See the discussions of case mapping in the Unicode Standard for more information.

Usage:

  • To do a simple case folding, use the mappings with status C + S.

  • To do a full case folding, use the mappings with status C + F.

    The mappings with status T can be used or omitted depending on the desired case-folding behavior. (The default option is to exclude them.)

Having no sense of the language of the text, Perl must exercise the default option of excluding the Turkic case folding.

And since Perl put in the effort to support full case foldings, it returns this one.

  1. The other character with a special folding is U+0049 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I.

    Status Use Fold
    C For full and simple implementations U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I
    T For Turkic languages, optionally U+0131 LATIN SMALL LETTER DOTLESS I

A concept is a named constraint. Your concept is

template<typename T>
concept Printable = requires(T obj) {
    { obj.print() } -> std::same_as<void>;
};

answers.body:
Domination is a relationship between the patterns themselves. The selector expression does not matter.

(Whether or not the type of the selector expression should be considered for determining dominance is another matter, and outside of the scope of this answer.)

As Jon Skeet said in the comments,

"Any value that will match for a byte will also match for a boxed Integer." Is that actually the case? What about a boxed Byte?

From the preview spec, the Integer pattern does not dominate the byte pattern. The relevant quotes are

(14.11.1)

A case label with a case pattern q is dominated if there is a preceding unguarded case label in the switch block with a case pattern p, and p dominates q

(14.30.3)

A pattern p dominates a type pattern that declares a pattern variable of type T if p is unconditional for T.

A type pattern that declares a pattern variable of a type S is unconditional for a type T if there is a testing conversion that is unconditionally exact (5.7.2) from |T| to |S|.

None of these definitions refer to the selector expression of the switch.

For this case, we can substitute Integer for "S" and byte for "T" into the last quote, and show that there is no testing conversion that is unconditionally exact from byte to Integer.

The unconditionally exact testing conversions are (5.7.2):

  • an identity conversion
  • an exact widening primitive conversion
  • a widening reference conversion
  • a boxing conversion
  • a boxing conversion followed by a widening reference conversion

To convert from byte to Integer, we need an (exact) widening primitive conversion followed by a boxing conversion, which is not in the above list.

79761108.body:
JEP 455 introduced Primitive Types in Patterns, instanceof, and switch as a preview feature in JDK 23. It continues as a preview feature in JDK 24 and 25, so the feature is not detailed in the Java Language Specification.

The JEP describes "safety of conversions", where certain pairs of types are unconditionally exact, meaning no runtime checks are required. For other pairs, a runtime test is necessary to determine if a conversion can be made without loss of information.

For example:

int x = getValue();  // Which returns 42

switch (x) {
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
}

The runtime check verifies that 42 will fit in a byte and matches, printing 'byte'.

If we change the order of the cases:

switch (x) {
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This will result in a compiler error because the int case now dominates the byte case.

Quoting from the Java Language Specification (where pattern dominance is defined),

A switch label in a switch block is said to be dominated if for every value that it applies to, it can be determined that one of the preceding switch labels would also apply.

So far, everything makes sense.

However, if we change the case for int to use the wrapper class Integer:

switch (x) {
  case Integer -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This code will compile without an error, and the result will be 'int'.

The compiler is clearly autoboxing the int to an Integer and matching the first case.

What I can't understand is why the compiler allows this, since the Integer case is still dominating the byte case. Any value that will match for a byte will also match for a boxed Integer.

JEP 507, the latest version states:

Furthermore, boxing conversions and widening reference conversions are unconditionally exact.

However, that still does not explain why the compiler is not rejecting this because of pattern dominance.

Just to be clear, all the examples use the same line, int x = getValue();, where getValue() returns 42.
79761108.title: Primitive types in patterns: why doesn't Integer dominate byte?

The Problem

I am trying to run a Flutter app on an iOS Simulator, but I'm getting the following error:

Runner's architectures (Intel 64-bit) include none that iPhone Air can execute (arm64).

Although the main Architectures setting in Xcode is set to arm64, the build fails because the simulator requires the arm64 architecture, and the app's build settings are somehow excluding it.

The Cause

This issue is caused by a misconfiguration in Xcode's Excluded Architectures build setting for the iOS Simulator. Although the project is correctly configured to build for arm64, the Excluded Architectures setting explicitly tells Xcode to ignore the arm64 architecture for the simulator, creating a direct conflict that prevents the app from running.

The Solution

To fix this, you must clear the incorrect architectures from the Excluded Architectures setting.

  1. Open your project in Xcode.

  2. Navigate to the Runner target by clicking on the project file in the left-hand navigator, and then selecting the Runner target.

  3. Go to the Build Settings tab.

  4. Use the search bar to find Excluded Architectures.

  5. Expand the Excluded Architectures section.

  6. Locate the row for Any iOS Simulator SDK and double-click the value to edit it.

  7. A pop-up window will appear. Select and delete any listed architectures (e.g., i386 and arm64). The list should be completely empty.

After completing these steps, go to Product > Clean Build Folder from the Xcode menu, and then try to build and run your application on the simulator. This should resolve the architecture mismatch error.

# /backend/utils/password.py

import hashlib
import bcrypt


_BCRYPT_ROUNDS = 12


def _sha256_hexdigest_bytes(password: str) -> bytes:
    return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest().encode()


def get_password_hash(password: str) -> str:
    """Hash password using bcrypt of SHA256-hexdigest(password).

    Returns a standard bcrypt hash string (e.g., "$2b$12$...").
    """
    prehashed = _sha256_hexdigest_bytes(password)
    salt = bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=_BCRYPT_ROUNDS)
    hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(prehashed, salt)

    return hashed.decode()


def verify_password(plain_password: str, hashed_password: str) -> bool:
    """Verify password against stored hash.

    Tries legacy prehashed mode first (sha256-hexdigest -> bcrypt). If that fails, it
    falls back to checking plain bcrypt (no pre-hash). Any ValueError from bcrypt
    (e.g., due to >72 byte inputs in plain mode) is treated as a failed check.
    """
    hp_bytes = hashed_password.encode()

    # 1) Preferred / legacy-compatible path: sha256-hexdigest -> bcrypt
    prehashed = _sha256_hexdigest_bytes(plain_password)
    if bcrypt.checkpw(prehashed, hp_bytes):
        return True

    # 2) Fallback: plain -> bcrypt (only if some old records used plain bcrypt)
    try:

        return bcrypt.checkpw(plain_password.encode(), hp_bytes)

    except ValueError:
        # bcrypt v5 raises if input >72 bytes (instead of silently truncating)

        return False

The problem is that you are using volatile keyword, which is exactly makes all the things are terrible to begin with.

So, what is actually happening behind the code that you wrote and optimizations that happens in the background :
The x86 compiler was smarter than the ARM compiler. Look at your assembly code.

  • x86 Release: The instruction addq $-2, %rdx means it handles 2 loop iterations at a time.

  • ARM Release: The instruction add x1, x1, #1 means it handles only 1 loop iteration at a time.

Even though your Mac is "emulating" the x86 code, it is emulating a more efficient version of your program (fewer checks, fewer jumps) than the native one.

2. Why is everything slow?
Because count is volatile, the CPU has to wait for memory to save the value after every single math operation. This bottleneck is so huge that it hides the usual differences between Debug and Release builds.

So, please check your code without volatile to actually check the CPU speed.

answers.body:
How does PostgreSQL decide when to switch from a custom plan to a generic plan for a prepared statement

Take a look at the Notes section in the PREPARE doc:

The current rule for this is that the first five executions are done with custom plans and the average estimated cost of those plans is calculated. Then a generic plan is created and its estimated cost is compared to the average custom-plan cost. Subsequent executions use the generic plan if its cost is not so much higher than the average custom-plan cost as to make repeated replanning seem preferable.

This heuristic can be overridden, forcing the server to use either generic or custom plans, by setting plan_cache_mode to force_generic_plan or force_custom_plan respectively.

Aside from checking your plan_cache_mode setting, you can take a look at the .generic_plans and .custom_plans counters in pg_prepared_statements system view to see what you were dealing with.

There's at most a single "switch", from custom to generic plan: if you're seeing pg_prepared_statements.generic_plans go up and explain shows $ params, you'll have to deallocate and prepare it again to change it (a schema change, like altering a column type can also trigger a re-plan). The moment Postgres determines that re-using an already form generic plan is cheaper than custom ones are, plus their planning cost, it'll no longer try those, so they won't get a chance to drop in cost and win back the position.

The thing to note in src/backend/utils/cache/plancache.c:1152 responsible for this is that num_custom_plans and total_custom_cost freeze the moment generic_cost wins, so from that point onward generic_cost will just keep winning.
(edited for brevity)

static bool
choose_custom_plan(CachedPlanSource *plansource, ParamListInfo boundParams)
{
    double      avg_custom_cost;
    if (plansource->is_oneshot)/* One-shot plans will always be considered custom */
        return true;
    if (boundParams == NULL)/* Otherwise, never any point in a custom plan if there's no parameters */
        return false;
    if (!StmtPlanRequiresRevalidation(plansource))/* ... nor when planning would be a no-op */
        return false;
    /* Let settings force the decision */
    if (plan_cache_mode == PLAN_CACHE_MODE_FORCE_GENERIC_PLAN)
        return false;
    if (plan_cache_mode == PLAN_CACHE_MODE_FORCE_CUSTOM_PLAN)
        return true;
    /* See if caller wants to force the decision */
    if (plansource->cursor_options & CURSOR_OPT_GENERIC_PLAN)
        return false;
    if (plansource->cursor_options & CURSOR_OPT_CUSTOM_PLAN)
        return true;
    if (plansource->num_custom_plans < 5)/* Generate custom plans until we have done at least 5 (arbitrary) */
        return true;
    avg_custom_cost = plansource->total_custom_cost / plansource->num_custom_plans;
    if (plansource->generic_cost < avg_custom_cost)
        return false;
    return true;
}

They normally grow with each new custom plan, which simply stop getting spawned.

why can that make performance worse for skewed data

Populate the table first, add indexing, consider adding extended stats, then analyze before allocating the prepared statement. Presence of data and an index on it doesn't mean pg_stats is already equipped to properly support the planner in its job, so you might potentially be freezing a suboptimal plan.

No amount of vacuum, analyze, create index, reindex, cluster, create statistics, or alter table..alter column..set statistics that normally help the planner, will affect an already prepared statement, which already elected a generic plan - unless you use force_custom_plan, auto decided to stick to custom (re-)planning on its own, or some DDL triggered a re-plan the pushed it below avg_custom_cost.

The performance problem you saw doesn't really stem from the data being skewed but more likely from the plan being formulated and frozen at a time the skew wasn't yet clear to the planner. After all, the newer faster plan was made by that exact same planner, just using more recent and improved stats - which suggests that if you were to re-allocate the statement now, the inferior, generic plan would be unlikely to win.

If the internal planner can now come up with an improved custom plan, it might be able to come up with an improved generic plan as well, or at least make a better informed decision to stick to custom ones.

About the idea to move plan selection off the db:

Just don't forget Postgres already has a planner built-in, and that's exactly its entire job that it can only do well if it's well-informed. If you're sure you can:

  1. Clearly define distinct variants of the same query and confirm they benefit from different plans.
  2. Decide which one to use, faster than the planner can just make a fresh plan (~70μs in your MRE).
  3. Define the rules behind that selection, and track what they depend on/their input better than the built-in statistics system and cluster config.
  4. Confirm 1-3 above successfully outperform the built-in planner.
  5. Confirm all 5 points here remain static: rules, required query variants and data profile aren't supposed to change.

Then it could be worthwhile. It would still be a heavily simplified re-implementation of what the built-in planner is already capable of, but if you find it's easier to do that than to convince it to do it for you, then it's a perfectly viable workaround. In your example, that would mean allocating 2 separate statements, the "rare" one being the addition:

PREPARE get_events_account_1 (smallint) AS
SELECT id, created_at, amount
FROM invoice_events
WHERE account_id = 1
  AND event_type = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

And you need to communicate if you're after the generic or the custom plan by switching plan_cache_mode accordingly. If you also use, or plan to use routines, they also cache plans.

Most of your potential performance gains can get completely nullified not just by a major version upgrade, but even a minor one, or a slight shift in your data profile, a tiny addition to your business logic.

Developing and maintaining this sort of feature might very well turn out to require a much larger effort than migrating to a more recent version, or taking a moment to try alternative partitioning, indexing and querying strategies, revisiting (de-)normalisation, tablespaces, compression and storage modes, tuning the cluster config - obviously, all after making sure the methods of aiding the internal planner mentioned and linked earlier, are exhausted.

The built-in planner reacts to any of these naturally. A "DIY plan picker" would have to be subjected to constant re-evaluation and manual adjustment.

By default (plan_cache_mode=auto), PostgreSQL starts with a custom plan and can switch the plan to generic anytime based on a formula on average cost estimations observed. So if you get a value that is not less selective than the previous one, it will think it has find a good generic plan. It hard-codes 5 custom executions before applying this formula in order to get something to average. So if you run more than five times it can change any time.

You should not use a prepared statement with parameters for columns with skew. It's like asking for a generic plan when you know there is no good generic plan. Or if you do, either:

  • force a custom plan rather than this auto switch which can happen any time after the fith execution.
  • force generic plan if the generic plan is good enough for all values

The best, if from the application you know when you use a parameter that has a different cardinality (for example from the use case you know if it's a low-volume account), is to use a different prepare statement for different scenarios.

That's the theory, but looking at you example, because you have the best index for pagination, an index scan should be good for all cases as it reads only 20 rows.

It seems that PG15 does a bitmap scan which doesn't preserve the order https://dbfiddle.uk/GkusTM0H

and in addition to that it doesn't estimate the cardinality correctly, even for the high-volume account.

The best you can do in my opinion (besides upgrading to PG18 which seems to do better here, but can still be subject to this) is disable bitmap scan (set enable_bitmapscan to off) for this query, as you know your index is the best for an index scan, and force a generic plan (set plan_cache_mode to force_generic_plan). Unfortunately, PostgreSQL has no hints (without pg_hint_plan extension) so be sure that you set that only for this query and don't leave such setting for others. a set local is better as the scope is the transaction.

Use a single Prepared Statements when data is normal

In general prepared statements are optimized for the case where a single plan performs reasonably well for all possible bind-parameter-values. In this case you can simply use a single prepared statement and the optimizer will find a generic plan, which will handle all possible parameter values well.

Use several Prepared Statements when you have a deciding column

Sometimes your data may be classified by one of the parameters and your statement will execute wildly different depending on this parameter. Example: SELECT * FROM transaction WHERE user = ? AND status = ? - May have significantly different plans for status = 'pending' (only a few transactions) and status = 'done' (whole history of transactions).

In this case the best course of action is usually to create multiple prepared statements for different values of status (a finite amount of statements, since status can only have a few distinct values). Each prepared statement can then use an optimized generic plan for the type of status. SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE user = ? and status = 'pending'

Use individual Statements or custom_plans for skewed data

If your data is heavily skewed and some parameter combinations perform vastly different then others, there will be no single generic plan which can handle all your calls. And you will also not be able to easily differentiate the call to multiple prepared statements.

In this case the best way is usually using individual statements instead of prepared statements (since a new plan needs to be computed for each combination of parameters anyway). Or you can use the option from the other answer and set the query planner to "custom_plans" for your prepared statement, so it will calculate a new custom plan each time.

If the slow performance calls are very few, you could also write a controller, which measures performance of a the prepared statement and marks the individual parameters in a map, so future calls with these parameters will be routed by your code to an individual single statement instead of the prepared statement, which handles all other calls.

    (random() * 1000)::numeric(12,2)

This is the solution that worked for me. Someone posted it here as an answer, but it was deleted, so I’m sharing it in case it helps others.

Tabs style objects don’t accept className, but tabBarBackground renders a normal component, so a View with className works and uses the @theme color directly:


<Tabs
  screenOptions={{
    headerShown: false,
    tabBarStyle: {
      position: "absolute",
      bottom: 25,
      left: 20,
      right: 20,
      height: 72,
      elevation: 0,
    },
    tabBarBackground: () => (
      <View className="flex-1 bg-foreground rounded-4xl" />
    ),
  }}
>
  {/* your Tabs.Screen items */}
</Tabs>

Tailwind CSS variables declared in @theme are intended to make Tailwind utilities available through those variables. If you never use a utility like text-primary or bg-primary anywhere in your code, the --color-primary variable won't be included in the generated CSS, even if you've declared it. You can verify this by inspecting the generated CSS.

If there's a chance you'll need to use the variable directly without referencing it through a Tailwind utility, you should use @theme static instead of @theme. This ensures that --color-primary is always included in the generated CSS and remains available as a CSS custom property, even if you never use it in a utility like bg-primary.

  • Trouble with Dynamic Color in Tailwind Component
  • Generating all CSS variables
@theme static {
  --color-primary: #081126;
  --color-accent: #ea7a53;
  --color-background: #fff9e3;
}

Since the backgroundColor property in the tabBarStyle object expects a valid CSS color value. On the web, you can use var(--color-primary) directly as a CSS color value:

<Tabs
  screenOptions={{
    tabBarStyle: {
      backgroundColor: "var(--color-primary)",
    },
  }}
>
  ...
</Tabs>

However, this approach is not guaranteed to work on native platforms (iOS and Android).

NativeWind provides an experimental useUnstableNativeVariable() hook that reads the resolved value of a CSS variable from the current variable context. You can use it to retrieve both colors and pass them to the corresponding React Native props:

import { useUnstableNativeVariable } from "nativewind";

function TabLayout() {
  const primary = useUnstableNativeVariable("--color-primary");

  return (
    <Tabs
      screenOptions={{
        tabBarStyle: {
          backgroundColor: primary,
        },
      }}
    >
      ...
    </Tabs>
  );
}

The property tabBarActiveTintColor and tabBarInactiveTintColor (edit: tabBarActiveIndicatorColor, tabBarRippleColor) provide the colors for the tabBarIcon and tabBarLabel which we can specify in the options prop of Tab.screen. You haven't specified that.

  • Setting the property tabBarActiveTintColor in Tab.Navigator does not work
import { useUnstableNativeVariable } from "nativewind";

function TabLayout() {
  const primary = useUnstableNativeVariable("--color-primary");
  const accent = useUnstableNativeVariable("--color-accent");

  return (
    <Tabs
      screenOptions={{
        tabBarStyle: {
          backgroundColor: primary,
          tabBarActiveTintColor: accent,
          tabBarInactiveTintColor: accent,
        },
      }}
    >
      {tabs.map((tab) => (
        <Tabs.Screen
          key={tab.name}
          name={tab.name}
          options={{
            tabBarIcon: ({ color }) => (
              <Ionicons name={tab.icon} size={32} color={color} />
            ),
          }}
        />
      ))}
    </Tabs>
  );
}

Does this filter before transfer or after?

The filter is applied on the server before data transfer. loadTable() returns a server-side table handle, .select() and .where() construct the query, and .to_pandas() transfers the filtered result to Python. Only the selected columns (sym, price) for rows matching date=2025.01.01 are returned, not the entire table.

loadTable() returns a server-side table handle. it does not eagerly transfer the entire table to Python. Chaining .select() and .where() performs the query on the server, and .to_pandas() transfers the resulting data to the client.

loadTable(tableName, dbPath=None, partitions=None, memoryMode=False)

loadTable is similar to table, but it can only be used to load tables on the server. It returns a table handle.

Similarly, Session.loadTable() returns a Table object. It does not upload local data; it obtains a handle to a table on the DolphinDB server.

Official Doc : Python API Reference Guide : Loading Data
Official Doc : Python API Reference Guide : Session.loadTable

Therefore, filtering with .where() before .to_pandas() avoids transferring the entire table to Python. Only the query result is transferred, although the server may still need to scan data internally.

In Rails 8 Propshaft will load .manifest.json from memory at startup. Even if you run assets:precompile and the manifest file is updated, Rails will continue to use the old manifest until the app gets restarted.

The most proper way to solve the issue is to compile the assets and then gracefully restart the application.

RAILS_ENV=production bin/rails assets:precompile
bundle exec pumactl phased-restart

This second command works only in case Puma is configured for phased restarts.

In case you don’t want to restart the whole app, you should reload the Propshaft asset resolver in every Rails process that is currently running. Unfortunately, there is no officially documented API provided by Propshaft that allows doing this.

And Rails.cache.clear won’t help because the manifest is stored in memory.

Recommendation: Perform a graceful restart after compiling the assets.

answers.body:
The reset triggered by the system when the launcher comes up, So you can not really stop. Listening for the change and re applying your configurations after the transition settles. You restore flashed and reverted back because it ran before the system finished resetting.

Example:

class VisionService : AccessibilityService() {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    private val scale = 1.5f

    private val listener = MagnificationController.OnMagnificationChangedListener { _, _, cfg ->
        if (cfg.scale != scale) handler.postDelayed({ apply() }, 300)
    }

    override fun onServiceConnected() {
        magnificationController.addListener(listener, handler)
        apply()
    }

    private fun apply() {
        val cur = magnificationController.magnificationConfig
        if (cur.scale == scale) return
        val cfg = MagnificationConfig.Builder()
            .setMode(MagnificationConfig.MAGNIFICATION_MODE_FULLSCREEN)
            .setScale(scale)
            .setCenterX(cur.centerX)
            .setCenterY(cur.centerY)
            .build()
        magnificationController.setMagnificationConfig(cfg, false)
    }

    override fun onAccessibilityEvent(e: AccessibilityEvent) {}
    override fun onInterrupt() {}

    override fun onDestroy() {
        magnificationController.removeListener(listener)
        handler.removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

The postDelayed gives the system time to finish by its own and reset. The cur.scale == scale check prevents a re apply the loop.

Android doesn't let you keep it. Every time the app in front changes, Android 15 zooms full-screen magnification back out FullScreenMagnificationController.onUserContextChanged(). It doesn't matter which service set the zoom, and there is no API to turn that off.

A workaround is to set it again once the switch is done. One switch can trigger the zoom-out more than once, so reapply after the last window change instead of right away

private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
private val reapplyZoom = Runnable {
    magnificationController.setMagnificationConfig(config, true)
}

override fun onAccessibilityEvent(event: AccessibilityEvent) {
    if (event.eventType == AccessibilityEvent.TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED) {
        handler.removeCallbacks(reapplyZoom) // only the last event in a burst re-applies
        handler.postDelayed(reapplyZoom, 500)
    }
}

This is a known TestFlight behaviour: StoreKit's product metadata can come back in USD in TestFlight even when the tester's shopfront is another country, while Apple's purchase sheet still shows the correct local currency and the purchase uses it.

Others with similar issues: https://community.revenuecat.com/general-questions-7/testflight-ios-18-5-ui-shows-usd-but-purchase-sheet-shows-inr-6396

Development builds don't show it because they use the device's Sandbox Apple Account, whose region sets the price. TestFlight uses your real Apple account in the sandbox environment.

To confirm it's StoreKit and not the Flutter plugin, upload your standalone StoreKit 2 probe to TestFlight as well, and log the Storefront.current's countryCode and the product's priceFormatStyle.currencyCode. If it returns USD there, there's nothing to fix in your app
